To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a vector-based vaccine that elicits rapid and sustained T effector cell responses in macaques controls the infection, and that a vaccine that elicits broadly neutralizing antibodies may provide protection from HIV-1 infection.

a vector-based viral vector vaccine that elicits an effective T cell response can be used in combination with a vaccine that elicits antibodies that block viral infection to achieve a protective response against HIV.

(1) a vector-based vaccine that elicits persistent and rapid T-effector cell response to HIV-1 antigens results in durable SIVmac239 infection control in 50% of rhesus macaque recipients; (2) the T-cell response to the SIVmac239 Gag protein is the main correlate of the protective effect; (3) a vaccine strategy that elicits a T-cell response to HIV-antigens is a promising approach to develop an HIV vaccine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of an effective antibody response, which will be the most effective weapon to prevent and stop the HIV/AIDS epidemic.
the design of a vaccine that will induce a strong and persistent T cell response, which will control the virus, and also a potent humoral response, which will prevent transmission.
the generation of a protective immune response to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which is the cause of the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a successful HIV vaccine should elicit both a humoral and a cellular response to prevent HIV infection.   1.
a successful HIV vaccine should be a two-pronged attack: one to control the infection and another to prevent it.
both arms are necessary for a successful vaccine.

a vaccine against HIV will need a robust cellular and a potent antibody response to be effective.
